forces: Soprano solo, mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Lisa della Casa, soprano; Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: Live, 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg
question: How does the same prayer change when it passes from one line to many?
intro: Low reeds and displaced string pulses prepare a prayer that gradually fills the choir. This is the Requiem movement Mozart left fully orchestrated; the surrounding work survives through other hands. Walter’s Salzburg performance lets the opening expand, withdraw for a soprano psalm verse and recover its choral weight.

sections.mNote: Imitative wind lines above displaced string pulses

sections.label: A · Choral prayer
sections.mNote: The opening idea becomes overlapping vocal entries

cues.title: A dark wind colour
cues.text: The score opens with bassoons and basset horns, low members of the reed family, rather than flutes or oboes. Their overlapping phrases emerge above short, displaced string pulses. Listen for a line beginning before its predecessor has finished.
cues.evidence: NMA completion volume, pp. 37–38; Breitkopf score, pp. 1–2. These are opening-score observations, not a claim that the transfer separately reveals every instrument. The report places a quiet introduction before the rise around 0:45–0:52.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Weight without a heavy beat
cues.text: Follow the short string notes underneath the longer wind lines. Their off-beat placement unsettles the tread: the accompaniment keeps moving even when the melody seems to hang in the air.
cues.evidence: The introduction’s string parts contain rests and displaced attacks. The report supports a gradually rising opening passage, not a beat-by-beat or instrument-isolated timing.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The prayer gathers voices
cues.text: Across the first choral span, the voices enter in succession instead of presenting the prayer as one solid block. Keep the first vocal line in mind while the others join: imitation makes the texture grow from within.
cues.evidence: The score’s initial choral entries follow the instrumental introduction; NMA pp. 39–40. The 0:52 novelty boundary and the sustained rise after 0:45 provisionally locate this change. No individual entrance is aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mozart’s completed opening
cues.text: Mozart dies in December 1791 before finishing the Requiem. The Introitus is the exception: he leaves it fully orchestrated. That distinction matters when we later reach music that Süssmayr has to extend or assemble.
cues.evidence: Leopold Nowak’s NMA preface distinguishes the completed Introitus from the incomplete later movements: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf. This is movement-wide context.

cues.title: A broad first crest
cues.text: The first choral span reaches a broad crest rather than one isolated accent. Notice how long the pressure is sustained before the sound retreats: the phrase’s duration is part of its weight.
cues.evidence: The report’s highest early five-second relative-level windows lie at 1:25, 1:30 and 1:35, followed by a lower level around 1:40. These are comparisons within this recording only.

cues.title: Space for one voice
cues.text: The choral prayer gives way to a quiet instrumental link and a soprano psalm verse. The change is not simply a softer version of the same texture: a single singer can carry a connected line where the choir has layered several.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 41–43: wind link followed by the soprano Te decet. The report shows a pronounced withdrawal around 2:05 and a quiet 2:10–2:20 span. The section includes the link; 2:06 is not asserted as the soprano’s entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The accompaniment stays alive
cues.text: In the psalm verse, listen beneath the soprano’s sustained syllables. The violin writing keeps moving in smaller notes, so repose in the vocal line does not mean the whole ensemble has become still.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 41–43 and Breitkopf pp. 4–5 show the soprano against active strings. The report’s changing texture at 2:30–2:56 supports this broad placement; it does not identify a particular syllable or violin attack.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A private memorial commission
cues.text: The Requiem begins as a commission associated with Count Franz von Walsegg’s memorial for his wife. Its familiar place in the concert hall comes later. The Latin words belong to a service for the dead, not a drama written about Mozart’s own death.
cues.evidence: The commission and memorial history are discussed in Nowak’s NMA preface and Jan Swafford’s programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/mozart-requiem. No deathbed scene is inferred from the music.

cues.title: The choir surrounds the solo
cues.text: The psalm does not remain a solo island. The chorus takes over, with broad vocal notes above continuing string motion. Compare this fuller texture with the more exposed soprano line that precedes it.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 43–44 gives the choral continuation of the psalm. The report shows the level rising around 3:00–3:15, then withdrawing sharply near 3:40. The timing is a passage estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first prayer returns
cues.text: The words of the opening prayer return after the psalm. This time, listen for the lines threading past one another: familiar material can sound more urgent when several voices are at different points in the same thought.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 45–46 restores Requiem aeternam with imitative vocal writing. The 3:38 boundary and quiet 3:40 window followed by renewed growth anchor the return provisionally; no first sung word is timestamped.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow a line through the crowd
cues.text: Choose a lower vocal line and try to keep it in view as higher voices overlap it. The texture is not melody plus a neutral accompaniment: several parts carry recognisable fragments while the orchestra reinforces their motion.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 46–47 shows the interweaving vocal and instrumental parts. This is a strategy for the returning choral passage, not a claim to have separated voices from the historical recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Salzburg, not a studio session
cues.text: This performance takes place in Salzburg’s Small Festival Hall on 26 July 1956. The Vienna Philharmonic’s archive lists Walter, the soloists and organist Franz Sauer. The programme also includes Mozart’s Symphony No. 25.
cues.evidence: Primary concert record: https://www.wienerphilharmoniker.at/en/konzerte/salzburg-festival/512/. Internet Archive describes the recording as live. The performance date is not treated as a record-release or transfer date.

cues.title: A second sustained weight
cues.text: The returning prayer builds another substantial crest. Hear it against the earlier one: the movement renews its force after a long withdrawal rather than pursuing one uninterrupted crescendo.
cues.evidence: The report shows high relative level around 4:30–4:40 and 5:00–5:05, followed by a large drop at 5:10. The cue concerns the extended later crest, not a single climax note.

cues.title: An ending that points onward
cues.text: The final prayer for light becomes quiet, but the score does not settle on a final D-minor tonic. It holds the dominant, A, and asks for the Kyrie to follow. This file ends at that suspended threshold; the Kyrie is not included here.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 48 ends on A with a fermata and attacca; Breitkopf p. 8 prints the following Kyrie. The report’s low final span begins near 5:10 and continues to the 338.38-second file end. The harmony is read from the score, not the machine key labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The wind idea becomes a choral entry
transitions.how: The instrumental opening establishes D minor and a chain of overlapping phrases. The choral basses begin the prayer and the other voices enter successively, taking up the same imitative principle. Short string gestures become a more forceful accompaniment as the vocal texture accumulates. The join enlarges material already present; it does not introduce an unrelated choral tune.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 37–40; Breitkopf pp. 1–3. The 0:52 report boundary follows the rise around 0:45–0:50. The join is provisional and does not align the individual choral entries.

transitions.title: A quiet link opens the psalm
transitions.how: The choir releases its opening prayer and the texture thins to an instrumental link. The score moves into the B♭ major region before the soprano begins the psalm verse. Active violin figures then surround a single vocal line; the low accompaniment is reduced, including an instruction to leave the organ out beneath the solo. Register and scoring, as well as the gentler harmonic setting, make the change audible.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 41–43, including the solo and senza organo indication. The report’s 2:06 boundary and low 2:05–2:20 span locate the link, not the solo’s precise entrance or a measured modulation.

transitions.title: The psalm gives back the opening words
transitions.how: The choral psalm continuation withdraws before the opening prayer returns. Its imitative material grows again from a thinner texture, with vocal lines and small instrumental figures overlapping. The return restores the movement’s D-minor direction without simply replaying its first orchestral introduction. The listener recognises the prayer through its contour and counterpoint, while its new placement gives it the weight of a response.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 44–46. The report has a 3:38 novelty boundary, low level at 3:40 and a subsequent rise. These locate the broad restart; the score, not chroma estimates, establishes the returning material.

transitions.title: The full prayer leaves a suspended chord
transitions.how: The accumulated choral weight recedes into the final request for light. Shorter moving figures give way to longer notes, and the bass approaches A rather than a closing D. Mozart holds that dominant harmony under a fermata and marks the continuation attacca. This is a half-close leading to the Kyrie in the full work, not a self-contained final tonic.
transitions.evidence: NMA p. 48; Breitkopf p. 8. The report’s 5:10 boundary and abrupt level fall anchor the closing withdrawal. The fermata and harmonic function are score observations; the following Kyrie is outside this file.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–8, checked against NMA pp. 37–48. Broad passage states, provisionally placed with the audio report; not aligned entrances or continuous playing. Basset horns have no stage token and are not mislabelled clarinets. Trombones are withheld: Nowak’s preface, p. XX n. 53, reports Walter cutting choral doublings, without a session-specific map.

timeline.note: The score opens with a low reed line and displaced strings; the low staff is marked solo and tasto solo, not a full organ chord.
Across the introduction both violin parts join the pulse beneath overlapping low winds; unrepresented basset horns are important here.
Successive choral entries build the prayer; trumpets and timpani punctuate the growing texture rather than sounding continuously.
A quieter wind-and-string link separates the first choral prayer from the soprano psalm.
The soprano psalm lies over moving violins and a reduced low line; the score explicitly withholds organ beneath the solo.
The choir resumes the psalm continuation while the strings retain their smaller moving figures.
The renewed prayer layers vocal lines and instrumental fragments; brass and drums provide intermittent weight.
The final span withdraws and lengthens towards the held dominant; the stage groups describe the scored passage, not a new tutti attack.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lisa della Casa (soprano), Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Mozart’s completed Introitus, within the traditional Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem; performing edition unidentified.
fields.note: The NMA distinguishes the Introitus, fully orchestrated by Mozart, from the incomplete later movements. The file contains this complete opening movement, stopping before the Kyrie. The traditional version is an identification from the repertory and score comparison, not an edition named by the upload. Walter’s precise instrumental alterations are unestablished.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
